characters: Sedinam: a 13-year-old girl in a school uniform with a clipboard, leading the debate.
Nii Armah: a 13-year-old boy in a school uniform, arguing that citizens must change first.
Aku: a 13-year-old girl in a school uniform, arguing that leaders are failing.
Mr Aryee: their social studies teacher, in a grey shirt, holding a folder of articles.

narrationPlan.voice: Brisk debate voices for the pupils; fair, steady voice for Mr Aryee
narrationPlan.pace: Brisk and fair, like a good debate (about 120 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Light, quick percussion for the debate, then a calm, thoughtful melody (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The pupils and teacher are invented. The facts come from engineers, studies and news features named in the fact-check.
This story is designed to teach balanced judgement: it neither blames only citizens nor only leaders.
Some of the cited sources are opinion pieces and should be shown to learners as opinions with evidence.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?

Check against named sources: many main drains designed for a 25-year flood; silt blocks drains first; over 52% of surveyed households name weak enforcement of land-use rules; two lagoons (Sakumo, Kpeshie) lost over 40% of their size; extreme rainfall events up 12% between 2010 and 2025.
Confirm the lagoon figure (it comes from a news feature’s own checks) and the 12% figure with the Ghana Meteorological Agency before release.
Check that Assembly Member is the correct local official to address and that the letter format is realistic.

teacherGuide.overview: A debate story that teaches evidence and balanced judgement. It shows that floods have several causes and that citizens and leaders both have duties.
learningGoals: Present arguments for and against a motion using evidence.
Explain why the honest answer to a hard question may include several causes.
Write a polite, factual letter to a local leader.
beforeReading: Hold a short mini-debate on a lighter motion to practise the rules.
whileReading: At page 5, ask learners to list all causes named and to sort them into “citizens” and “leaders” and “nature”.
afterReading: Write your own letter to the Assembly Member with a drain count.
Run your own debate and invite an adult to judge on evidence.
discussion: Why do people sometimes blame only one cause?
How can a polite letter be stronger than a loud complaint?
reflection: What is one thing you will do and one thing you will ask leaders to do?

mathsExtension.task: A main drain is designed for a 1-in-25-year flood. In 100 years, how many such floods would be expected on average?
Extreme rainfall events rose by 12%. If there were 50 in 2010, about how many in 2025?

support: Give learners a table: Cause / Who can act.
stretch: Find out how your local assembly decides which drains to clear.

culturalNotes: The pupils and teacher are invented. The facts come from engineers, studies and news features named in the fact-check.
This story is designed to teach balanced judgement: it neither blames only citizens nor only leaders.
Some of the cited sources are opinion pieces and should be shown to learners as opinions with evidence.
localiseThis: Use real local examples and invite an Assembly Member or assembly staff member to answer questions.
Keep the tone respectful when writing to leaders.

whatWeKnow: Silt, waste, wetland loss, small drains and heavier rain all contribute to Accra’s floods.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: How much each cause contributes; experts differ on this.

factCheck.claim: Many of Accra’s main drains were designed for a 25-year flood event; silt blocks drains first and traps debris; weak enforcement of wetland laws; lack of retention ponds; she disputes that plastic is the main blockage.
factCheck.explanation: An environmental engineer spoke on a television programme on 11 July 2026.
factCheck.reference: MyJoyOnline, “Accra floods driven more by poor drainage and silt than littering – Dr Ohemeng-Ntiamoah”.

factCheck.claim: Over 52% of surveyed households in flood-prone areas named weak enforcement of land-use regulations as the principal cause; wetlands and buffer zones have been encroached upon; drains are blocked by solid waste.
factCheck.explanation: From an opinion article by an environmental policy lecturer who cites a 2025 study of Accra.
factCheck.reference: Graphic Online, “Accra is not drowning by accident”.

factCheck.claim: Sakumo and Kpeshie lagoons lost over 40% of their size to encroachment; extreme rainfall events increased by 12% between 2010 and 2025 according to the Ghana Meteorological Agency; heavy rain of 60 to 80 mm in two hours.
factCheck.explanation: From a Ghana News Agency feature (figures as reported there).
factCheck.reference: Ghana News Agency, “Ghana’s flooding: women and children suffer needlessly” (4 July 2026).

pronunciation.guidance: Ghanaians often say "uh-KRAH" (stress on the second syllable).
